title: A hard hadith, read in context
hookLine: a hadith about fighting people until they testify, which scholars read as about the wars of its time, alongside no compulsion in religion
tomorrow: why avoid all of the wrong, but only some of the right?

lines: 'DO I HAVE TO HATE MY FRIEND?'
cards: After class, a ten-year-old holds up his big brother's phone. A clip: dark music, big white captions, a line from a hadith. I have been commanded to fight the people.
Then it cuts to black. He doesn't ask what it means. He asks, quietly, whether it means he's supposed to hate his friend from soccer.
Yesterday's question asked which hadith gets clipped and shared to scare people. This is the one, eighth in al-Nawawi's forty. And the clip stops right before the part that matters.

teach.b: Here's the whole report from Ibn Umar, in paraphrase.

The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said he was commanded to fight the people until they testify that there's no god but Allah and that he is Allah's messenger, establish the prayer and give zakat; and if they do, their lives and property are safe, except by the right of Islam, and their reckoning is with Allah.
Read in ten seconds, it sounds like a war on everyone. Now read it with the scholars. First: who are the people?

teach.h: 'THE PEOPLE': THE WARS OF ITS TIME.
teach.b: Commentators read the word here as a particular group, those then at war with the Muslims, in the wars of its time, not all of humankind. Second: the Qur'an, in Pickthall's translation.

"There is no compulsion in religion." Another verse says Allah doesn't forbid kindness and fair dealing toward those who don't fight you over religion. The scholars read the hadith inside those verses, not against them.
Third: the last line, the one the clip always cuts.
Their reckoning is with Allah. Outward words are accepted, and no one gets to put a heart on trial.
One to tell a friend tonight: a hard text read alone and the same text read with its scholars can be two different texts.

how: Muslim teachers read hard hadith with the classical commentaries and the Qur'an's verses on the same subject, and explain a report's setting before its meaning is applied.

o: a report with a weak chain that scholars reject
a report that must be learned by heart in Arabic
a report that's easy to misread without its context

games.q: the whole report — tap the pairs.
p: read as those then at war
stops before the part that matters

s: this hadith isn't in the major collections, so it can be ignored
it's in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim. the answer is to read it with its scholars, not to wish it away.
commentators read 'the people' here as every human being
they read it as a particular group: those then at war with the Muslims.
the report ends: their reckoning is with Allah
outward words are accepted. hearts are left to Allah.

games.q: a coworker forwards a quote card: half a verse from some scripture that sounds violent. what's the first move today's lesson suggests?
o: find the whole passage, and what its own scholars say about its setting.
share it with a warning, so people know what that faith really teaches.
ignore it completely: old texts have nothing to say about today.
games.why: a hard text read alone and the same text read with its scholars can be two different texts. the whole report first, then its setting.

practice: Say the verse out loud, slowly, in Pickthall's words: "There is no compulsion in religion." Say it a second time, more quietly.
Then sit with it beside the hard hadith, not cancelling it but holding it, the way the scholars hold the two together.

wordCard.voice: A hard hadith: a report that's easy to misread on its own. This one is read with its setting, its closing line, and the Qur'an's no compulsion in religion.

orig.note: Arabic, Qur'an 2:256: there is no compulsion in religion.

carryVoice: One line to carry: read it with the scholars, the whole report and its setting, never the clip alone. Ten days into the last range.
